title: Robin Hood Hashing Breaks: Interactive Hash-Table Race
pitch: Single-page canvas demo: insert keys into a quadratic-probing hash table under 'Robin Hood' ordering vs 'anti-Robin Hood' ordering side by side, with a load-factor slider. Watch probe-length histograms diverge — the 'fair' Robin Hood strategy visibly degrades to sqrt(1/eps) query time while the naive one stays near-log. Ends with a big red 'the textbooks were wrong' reveal.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — a decades-trusted 'fairness' heuristic in CS turns out to be the loser, which is catnip for the decision-theory crowd.

title: The Fairness Trick That Quietly Broke Your Hash Table
pitch: Explainer walking through smoothed analysis: why 'Robin Hood hashing' (steal probe-length from the rich, give to the poor) sounds obviously better but provably loses to dumb fixed-offset probing once you do the math properly. Good hook for anyone who's ever trusted an intuitive fairness rule over the numbers.
discussion_why: moderate discussion fit — appeals to the 'intuition vs math' debate that decision-theory nerds love, less so the betting crowd directly.

title: Smoothed-Analysis Hash Bench
pitch: Open-source JS/Python benchmark reproducing the paper's result: Robin Hood vs anti-Robin Hood vs FCFS probing across load factors, with live charts. A reusable artifact for anyone who wants to sanity-check their own hash table implementation choice.
discussion_why: solid nerd-utility but low shareability outside a narrow CS audience.

title: The Model Remembers You
pitch: Single-file HTML sandbox: train a tiny in-browser classifier on synthetic 'patient' records, then replay one patient with a new condition vs a genuinely new patient. Sliders for training epochs/overlap show accuracy silently sag for returning-but-changed cases while looking artificially great for returning-and-stable ones — the paper's memorisation bias made tangible in 30 seconds of play.
discussion_why: relatability wins — 'the AI that's supposed to help you can quietly get worse specifically because it remembers you' is an unsettling, shareable idea.

title: Sharp Detector: When the Book Remembers Your Action
pitch: Direct transplant of the medical-AI mechanism onto sportsbook line-setting: a toy model that has 'seen' a bettor before shades new lines worse for them (mirroring reduced sensitivity to new conditions) while looking deceptively accurate on their repeat behavior. Interactive HTML toy lets you toggle 'bettor seen in training' and watch the model's confidence and shading shift in real time.
discussion_why: direct hit on betting — gives the eternal 'sportsbooks limit sharps' paranoia an actual algorithmic mechanism to argue about.

title: Your AI Doctor Remembers You — And That Might Hurt You
pitch: Explainer on memorisation bias in clinical AI: why de-identified training data doesn't stop a model from silently favoring or failing you based on having seen your old records, and why nobody currently checks for this before deployment.
discussion_why: genuine 'wait, really?' surprise about a healthcare risk most people have never heard of.
